title: Is it an institution, digital or social inclusion that matters for inclusive growth? A panel data analysis
technology: digital inclusion index (internet users, broadband subscriptions, mobile users; min-max composite)
estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel), estimated separately by WB income group

contrasts.study: Is it an institution, digital or social inclusion that matters for inclusive growth? A panel data analysis
contrasts.outcome: inclusive growth index (composite; GDP per capita, employment ratio, income equality)
contrasts.evidence: Table 1 p.346: DI HYCs 0.0318* (SE 0.0171); LYCs 0.00382 (SE 0.0339); observations 174 / 168
contrasts.notes: Headline: DI, richest vs poorest income group, the study's main digital measure. No formal difference test. AR(2) and Hansen tests reported. Outcome combines output and distribution/employment components, coded families 1 and 4.

contrasts.study: Is it an institution, digital or social inclusion that matters for inclusive growth? A panel data analysis
contrasts.outcome: inclusive growth index (composite; GDP per capita, employment ratio, income equality)
contrasts.notes: Non-headline pair. No formal difference test.

contrasts.study: Is it an institution, digital or social inclusion that matters for inclusive growth? A panel data analysis
contrasts.outcome: inclusive growth index (composite; GDP per capita, employment ratio, income equality)
contrasts.notes: Both estimates insignificant; the difference is negligible. No formal difference test.

title: The Impact of Mobile Broadband and Internet Bandwidth on Human Development—A Comparative Analysis of Developing and Developed Countries
technology: mobile broadband, internet bandwidth, mobile basic and fixed broadband basic subscriptions
estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, HDI lag), estimated separately for developing (121) and developed (59) countries

contrasts.study: The Impact of Mobile Broadband and Internet Bandwidth on Human Development—A Comparative Analysis of Developing and Developed Countries
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, HDI lag)
contrasts.evidence: Table 2 col 1 (developing): 0.000074** (SE 0.000035), N 892, 120 countries; Table 3 col 1 (developed): -0.000039 (SE 0.000026), N 465, 59 countries
contrasts.notes: Headline: mobile broadband, the paper's main contrast (the mobile broadband result for developing countries is the abstract's headline). Baseline dynamic GMM; no formal difference test; developed effect not significant, developing effect significant. Opposite signs. Tables 6-7 (HDI dimensions) and Table 4-5 robustness not coded.

contrasts.study: The Impact of Mobile Broadband and Internet Bandwidth on Human Development—A Comparative Analysis of Developing and Developed Countries
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, HDI lag)
contrasts.notes: Non-headline. Developed estimate significant at 10%; developing estimate has a very large SE, so the point difference is not meaningful. No difference test.

contrasts.study: The Impact of Mobile Broadband and Internet Bandwidth on Human Development—A Comparative Analysis of Developing and Developed Countries
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, HDI lag)
contrasts.notes: Non-headline. Both insignificant. The paper drops mobile basic from further analysis after the developing-country baseline.

contrasts.study: The Impact of Mobile Broadband and Internet Bandwidth on Human Development—A Comparative Analysis of Developing and Developed Countries
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, HDI lag)

title: Strengthening economic resilience through ICT during the COVID-19 pandemic: evidence from 100 countries
technology: UNCTAD ICT index (fixed broadband, mobile subscriptions, secure servers), and its interaction with COVID-19 incidence
estimator: two-step system GMM with IV-GMM robustness; split by ICT intensity (developing 40, developed 60)

contrasts.study: Strengthening economic resilience through ICT during the COVID-19 pandemic: evidence from 100 countries
contrasts.technology: ICT index x COVID-19 deaths (mitigation interaction)
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, lagged growth), split by ICT intensity (Table 5)
contrasts.evidence: Table 5 (cols 2 and 5): Deaths*ICT developing 0.027*** (SE 0.003), developed 0.004** (SE 0.002); observations 240 / 360
contrasts.notes: Headline: mitigating effect of ICT on the COVID-19 death shock, the abstract's main claim. Split is by ICT intensity (median), not income: the authors label the groups developed/developing. Interaction coefficients are not a level effect of ICT. No difference test. Split by ICT intensity, not income: not an income contrast.

contrasts.study: Strengthening economic resilience through ICT during the COVID-19 pandemic: evidence from 100 countries
contrasts.technology: ICT index x COVID-19 cases (mitigation interaction)
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, lagged growth), split by ICT intensity (Table 5)
contrasts.notes: Non-headline. Same ICT-intensity split; no difference test. Split by ICT intensity, not income: not an income contrast.

contrasts.study: Strengthening economic resilience through ICT during the COVID-19 pandemic: evidence from 100 countries
contrasts.technology: ICT index x COVID-19 stringency (mitigation interaction)
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, lagged growth), split by ICT intensity (Table 5)
contrasts.notes: Non-headline. Point estimates equal at three decimals; no difference test. Split by ICT intensity, not income: not an income contrast.

contrasts.study: Strengthening economic resilience through ICT during the COVID-19 pandemic: evidence from 100 countries
contrasts.estimator: two-step system GMM (dynamic panel, lagged growth), split by ICT intensity (Table 5)
contrasts.evidence: Table 5 (col 2 developing 0.171, SE 0.074; col 5 developed -0.024, SE 0.050)
contrasts.notes: Non-headline. Main effect is the ICT effect when the death shock is zero in this specification, so it is hard to read as a growth effect. Neither estimate is significant at 10%; no stars printed. Split by ICT intensity, not income: not an income contrast.

title: Building a sustainable and innovative world in the digital age: A cross-country study
estimator: cross-sectional OLS linear regression, split by GDP per capita threshold (20,000 USD)

contrasts.study: Building a sustainable and innovative world in the digital age: A cross-country study
contrasts.outcome: SDG index score (composite of SDG outcomes including environmental goals)
contrasts.comparison: income level (GDP per capita threshold 20,000 USD)
contrasts.richer_group: high-income countries (GDP per capita above 20,000 USD)
contrasts.poorer_group: low-income countries (GDP per capita below 20,000 USD)
contrasts.evidence: Table 6: model 8 (high-income, n=36) GDI 0.183** (SE 0.081); model 7 (low-income, n=36) GDI 0.219*** (SE 0.080)
contrasts.notes: Headline: GDI, high vs low income by the authors' GDP per capita threshold. Point estimates are almost equal (the groups differ mainly in significance); no interaction or difference test. Regressions include GDP per capita, economic freedom and population density (not coded). Cross-sectional data, so 'n_obs' equals the number of countries. Environmental SDG goals are part of the outcome.

title: Impacts of the digital economy on industrial employment and CO2 emissions: a comparison between developed and developing countries
technology: ICT goods imports relative to total merchandise imports (log)
estimator: two-step system GMM (SYS-GMM), 3-equation system, estimated separately for 7 developed and 8 developing countries

contrasts.study: Impacts of the digital economy on industrial employment and CO2 emissions: a comparison between developed and developing countries
contrasts.outcome: industrial CO2 emissions (log; lower is better)
contrasts.technology: ICT goods imports relative to total merchandise imports (log)
contrasts.richer_group: developed countries (Canada, France, Germany, Israel, Italy, Japan, Spain)
contrasts.poorer_group: developing countries (Bahrain, Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Turkey)
contrasts.evidence: Table 5 (developed) Equation 3: lnICT_IMPORT -0.159 (SE 0.037, p<0.01); Table 6 (developing) Equation 3: -0.008 (SE 0.019, p 0.676)
contrasts.notes: Headline: CO2 family, the study's clearest contrast. Lower emissions are better, so the sign is reversed: developed-country ICT imports reduce CO2, developing-country imports do not, and direction is coded in benefit terms (richer larger). Country classification uses World Bank income, OECD membership and HDI (>= 0.800) for developed. No difference test. N not reported.

contrasts.study: Impacts of the digital economy on industrial employment and CO2 emissions: a comparison between developed and developing countries
contrasts.technology: ICT goods imports relative to total merchandise imports (log)
contrasts.richer_group: developed countries (Canada, France, Germany, Israel, Italy, Japan, Spain)
contrasts.poorer_group: developing countries (Bahrain, Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Oman, Saudi Arabia, Tunisia, Turkey)
contrasts.evidence: Table 5 (developed) Equation 1: lnICT_IMPORT -0.038 (SE 0.020, p 0.057); Table 6 (developing) Equation 1: -0.016 (SE 0.010, p 0.113)
contrasts.notes: Non-headline. Both negative. Employment is the benefit, so the developed-country negative effect is the larger harm: coded as poorer larger in benefit terms. Only the developed estimate is significant at 10%. No difference test. N not reported.
